name: Ginseng
subtitle: Panax ginseng - 50 vegan capsules x 800mg
standfirst: Panax ginseng, the root of a slow-growing perennial native to the cool forests of East Asia. Fifty vegan capsules to a pack, 800mg each, no fillers. Nothing else in the pack.
body: Panax ginseng is a slow-growing perennial in the Araliaceae family, native to the cool forests of Korea, north-east China and the Russian Far East. A wild root takes years to reach a size worth digging, which is why most ginseng sold today, this pack included, is cultivated rather than wild-dug.

The listing titles the product 'Ginseng (Siberian)' and then describes Panax ginseng the whole way down. Two different plants, wearing one name. Panax ginseng carries the ginsenosides; Siberian ginseng usually means Eleutherococcus senticosus, a different genus with a different chemistry entirely. We have put the question to Reiss directly: which one is actually in the capsule.
Each capsule is 800mg. Fifty to a pack. No fillers.
spec: Asian ginseng, Korean ginseng, Chinese ginseng
25 days on, 5 days off. As printed on the label
dose: Two capsules a day, morning or early afternoon, per the label.
supply: Fifty capsules. Two a day makes twenty five days, about three and a half weeks.
cautions: Not recommended in pregnancy or while breastfeeding.
Speak to your GP before taking this if you are on blood-thinning medication such as warfarin, or on blood pressure medication.
Speak to your GP before taking this if you have a hormone-sensitive condition.
If it disrupts your sleep, take it earlier in the day or lower the dose.

name: Chasteberry
subtitle: Vitex agnus-castus - 50 vegan capsules
standfirst: Vitex agnus-castus, a Mediterranean shrub of the mint family, its dried berry taken into fifty vegan capsules to a pack.
body: Vitex agnus-castus is a deciduous shrub native to the Mediterranean and central Asia, slender grey-green leaves, spikes of small violet flowers by late summer. The berry ripens dark and peppery, and that pepper is exactly where the old country name comes from: chaste tree, and on the trade shelf, monk's pepper.
The dried berry is what goes into the capsule. No weight per capsule is printed, no extraction ratio either, so how concentrated the fill actually is against the raw berry, we cannot say.
Fifty to a pack. Two a day, first thing, with water, is what the label recommends.
spec: 25 days on, 5 days off. As printed on the label
dose: Two capsules a day, first thing in the morning, before breakfast, with at least 500ml water.
supply: Fifty capsules. Two a day makes twenty five days, which is the supply printed on the label, then five days off.
cautions: Not recommended in pregnancy: the label advises stopping if you become pregnant. Speak to your GP.
Speak to your GP before taking this if you are on the contraceptive pill, hormone replacement therapy, or medication for Parkinson's disease or schizophrenia.
Speak to your GP before taking this if you are on any other prescribed medication.

name: Astragalus
subtitle: Astragalus membranaceus - 50 vegan capsules x 800mg
standfirst: Astragalus membranaceus, a perennial of the pea family grown across China for centuries. Fifty vegan capsules to a pack, 800mg each. No fillers, no bulking agents.
body: Astragalus membranaceus is a perennial of the pea family, growing to about a metre, feathery leaves, small pale yellow flowers. Native to northern and eastern China, Mongolia and Korea, where it has stood as a field crop for centuries.

Which part of the plant fills this pack, the listing does not say. Root is almost always the part used commercially; huang qi, the trade name, refers specifically to the dried root in Chinese medicine. We have asked Reiss to confirm it rather than assume it.
Fifty to a pack, 800mg each. No fillers, no bulking agents.

name: Gumbo Limbo
subtitle: Bursera simaruba - vegan capsules
standfirst: Bursera simaruba, a fast-growing tree of the Caribbean and Central America, known everywhere by its red, peeling bark. No capsule count on the listing, no weight, no stated part of the tree. Those questions go to Reiss; this entry stays short until they come back.
body: Bursera simaruba is a large tree native to the Caribbean, Central America and southern Florida, easy to spot by the thin, copper-red bark peeling off it in papery sheets, hence the local nickname, tourist tree, after the sunburnt visitors it resembles. It grows fast, and it grows from almost nothing: cut a branch, plant it, and it roots where it stands. Which is exactly why it turns up as a living fence post across the region.

Which part of the tree goes into the capsule, how many capsules make a pack, what each one weighs, the listing says none of it. Three questions, put to Reiss, before this page can carry a full specification.

name: Gotu Kola
subtitle: Centella asiatica - vegan capsules
standfirst: Centella asiatica, a low, creeping herb of the carrot family, found right across South and South East Asia. No capsule count printed, no weight, no stated part of the plant. Open questions, all three, for Reiss.
body: Centella asiatica is a small creeping perennial of the carrot family, fan-shaped leaves on long thin stalks, tiny pinkish flowers hidden close to the ground. It grows in wet, marshy ground across South and South East Asia, eaten fresh as a salad leaf in Sri Lanka and Indonesia, and dried for herbal use besides.
Leaves and stems together, the aerial parts, are what most commonly gets dried for a capsule. Whether that is actually what fills this pack, the listing never confirms. So we have asked.

name: Bugle
subtitle: Lycopus virginicus, as printed on the listing - vegan capsules
standfirst: Lycopus virginicus, the listing calls it, though the name printed on the front is Bugle, and bugle usually means a different plant entirely. We have asked Reiss to confirm which one is actually in the capsule.
body: Bugle is a common name with more than one owner. British herbal use gives it to Ajuga reptans, a low, spreading mint-family plant with blue flower spikes, common enough on damp woodland edges. American and continental use gives bugleweed to Lycopus virginicus, or its European relative Lycopus europaeus, mint family too but a different genus altogether, taller, favouring wet ground near streams and ditches.

This listing's title says Bugle. The text underneath says Lycopus Virginicus, calls it Bugleweed throughout, and never once says Ajuga. So Lycopus it is, on the name printed. But a mix-up like this is exactly the kind worth confirming before the page goes live.
No capsule count printed for this pack. No weight either.

name: Acacia Bark
subtitle: Acacia sp., species to be confirmed - 50 vegan capsules
standfirst: Acacia bark, and Acacia is a genus of well over a thousand species. Which one fills this pack, the listing never says, so the species stays an open question, not a guess. Fifty vegan capsules to a pack.
body: Acacia is one of the largest tree genera going, species native to Africa, Arabia, southern Asia, Australia. A handful are grown commercially for bark and resin. Acacia senegal and Acacia seyal supply most of the world's gum arabic, the hardened resin that seeps from a cut in the bark, used as a food thickener and, across North Africa and the Middle East, in traditional medicine besides.

The listing describes the tree only as 'the ancient Acacia tree native to the Indus Kush region, stretching from North Africa through Arabia into India', and it mentions gum arabic, which points toward Acacia senegal or a relative. But no binomial, anywhere on the listing. 'Acacia bark' can mean the bark of dozens of traded species, each with its own chemistry, so we have logged this as a query rather than picked one for you.
spec: Not stated. Genus is Acacia, species unconfirmed

name: Chanca Piedra
subtitle: Phyllanthus niruri - 800mg vegan capsules

body: Phyllanthus niruri is a small, upright annual, rarely taller than half a metre, feathery rows of tiny leaflets along thin stems, seed-like flowers sitting directly under each leaf. It grows widely through the Amazon basin and other tropical and subtropical ground, often as a weed of disturbed and cultivated land, and it carries a long history through South American herbal tradition.

Each capsule is 800mg of the extract. No fillers, no additives. Which part of the plant went into it, or whether it was the whole plant, the listing does not say, and it does not state how many capsules make up a pack either.

body: Withania somnifera is a small, woody shrub in the nightshade family, growing to about a metre, dull green oval leaves, small greenish-yellow flowers, round orange-red berries the size of a small pea held inside a papery husk. It grows across India, the Middle East and North Africa, and it has stood in Indian herbal medicine for centuries under its Sanskrit name, ashwagandha.
